Course-voice weekly lesson pages for the 15-week Intro to Statistics
spine. Each weekly page is the **main reading** for that week — a
short textbook-depth read that teaches the concepts end-to-end, with
outbound links to OpenIntro IMS and ISLBS for an alternate voice.

Every page follows the same shape: a warm-up question to think about
before you read, why the week's ideas matter, what you will be able to
do by the end of it, a table of the words to know, the concepts
themselves, two fully worked examples (three in Week 10), a transfer
example that carries the same reasoning into a new setting, the common
misreading to avoid, and ungraded practice questions, some with a note
on what to look for. Worked examples use small hypothetical data sets
chosen to make the reasoning visible; where that is the case, the page
says so.

## Available

- [Week 1 — Data, evidence, and statistics](week01-data-evidence.qmd) —
  treating data as evidence, and naming what data alone cannot
  establish; cases and variables in a data matrix; numerical and
  categorical variables, including ones recorded with number codes;
  explanatory and response variables; and choosing the summary that
  fits the comparison a claim rests on.
- [Week 2 — Study design, bias, and causality](week02-study-design.qmd) —
  observational studies and experiments; what random *sampling* and
  random *assignment* each allow you to conclude, placed on one
  scope-of-inference grid; convenience samples, voluntary response,
  and non-response, and which way each bias pushes; confounding; and
  what a control group, a placebo, and blinding add.
- [Week 3 — One-variable summaries](week03-one-variable-summaries.qmd) —
  dot plots, histograms, and box plots; describing a distribution by
  shape, center, spread, and unusual values; the mean, median,
  quartiles, IQR, and standard deviation by hand; the 1.5 × IQR rule;
  when to report the median instead of the mean; and counts and
  proportions for a categorical variable.
- [Week 4 — Comparing groups](week04-comparing-groups.qmd) —
  side-by-side box plots and dot plots read for center, spread, and
  overlap; differences in means and medians, with units and a
  direction; two-way tables, conditional proportions, and segmented
  bar charts; and the risk difference and relative risk, and why a
  report needs both.
- [Week 5 — Association](week05-association.qmd) — scatterplots read
  for direction, form, strength, and unusual observations; what the
  correlation measures, and computing it for a small data set; when a
  curve or one unusual point makes it mislead; association versus
  causation; and association between two categorical variables.
- [Week 6 — Confounding and multivariable thinking](week06-confounding.qmd) —
  how a third variable tied to both the explanatory and the response
  variable can distort a comparison; simple causal diagrams; comparing
  within strata; Simpson's paradox worked through two hospitals;
  adjusted rates as weighted averages; and what random assignment
  fixes that adjustment cannot.
- [Week 7 — First-half synthesis](week07-synthesis-midterm.qmd) —
  the first six weeks gathered into one six-step routine for reading
  a study from question to conclusion, worked end to end on a walking
  program for older adults and a randomized trial of a reduced-sodium
  diet, then carried to bike lanes and traffic deaths across cities.
- [Week 8 — Simple regression](week08-simple-regression.qmd) —
  the least-squares line, from output or from summary statistics; the
  slope and intercept read in context; residuals, the residual plot,
  and R²; extrapolation and when not to trust a prediction; and the
  estimate and standard error columns of regression output.
- [Week 9 — Multiple and logistic regression, by interpretation](week09-multiple-logistic-regression.qmd) —
  multiple regression output read as comparisons that hold the other
  variables fixed; why an adjusted slope can differ sharply from the
  unadjusted one; indicator variables as group differences; then
  probability, odds, and log odds, logistic coefficients as odds
  ratios, predicted probabilities, and why an odds ratio is not
  "times as likely."
- [Week 10 — Probability as risk and diagnosis](week10-probability-risk-diagnosis.qmd) —
  probability as a long-run relative frequency; conditional
  probability from a two-way table, and why P(A | B) is not P(B | A);
  absolute risk, relative risk, and the number needed to treat;
  sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values through natural
  frequencies; and why a positive test for a rare condition is often
  a false positive.
- [Week 11 — Simulation-based inference](week11-simulation-based-inference.qmd) —
  could chance alone have produced this? Sampling variability; a
  randomization test built by shuffling group labels, with its p-value
  as a proportion of shuffles; the bootstrap and a 95% percentile
  interval; what "95% confidence" does and does not mean; and which
  StatKey menu fits each question.
- [Week 12 — Classical hypothesis testing](week12-classical-hypothesis-testing.qmd) —
  the normal model as a shortcut to the Week 11 simulation: hypotheses
  stated before the data, the standard error and the *z* statistic,
  p-values and 95% confidence intervals for one and two proportions
  and for a mean, Type I and Type II errors and power, and statistical
  versus practical significance.
- [Week 13 — Categorical outcomes](week13-categorical-outcomes.qmd) —
  counts, proportions, and rates per 1,000 or per 100,000, and when a
  rate is the fair comparison; choosing the right conditional
  proportions in a two-way table; a confidence interval for the
  difference between two proportions; expected counts and the
  chi-square statistic; and what a significant chi-square result does
  and does not show.
- [Week 14 — Meta-analysis and forest plots](week14-meta-analysis-forest-plots.qmd) —
  how single studies become a body of evidence: effect sizes with
  confidence intervals, reading a forest plot, pooling by
  inverse-variance weighting, heterogeneity and the random-effects
  idea, publication bias and funnel plots, and writing a responsible
  conclusion. The studies are hypothetical, not results from real
  trials.
- [Week 15 — Final review](week15-final-review.qmd) — what claim can
  we responsibly make? The whole course as one chain of reasoning from
  question to conclusion, worked on a randomized walking program and
  on five trials of a supplement, then carried to a positive screening
  test; the common misreadings from across the course in one place;
  and practice that mixes the weeks. A review aid, not an exam preview.
